segments.text: Sorry, sorry, I don't want to make a fuss, but my chest has gone really tight, and the walk from the car park was far longer than I remembered. Is it always that far? I swear they've moved the entrance.
Let's get you sitting up properly. Sam, can you grab a chair with arms for him? Right, tell me about the tightness.
Here you go, love. Lean back, nice and easy.

Thanks. It's a tight chest, like someone's pulled a belt round it, and it always happens on cold days. It's been like that since the cold snap started last week, and today it's been worse than ever, I even had my scarf over my mouth.
And are you short of breath with it?

Yes, a bit. Well, a lot, on the stairs. And there's a whistling noise when I breathe out, my mate on the site said it sounded like a kettle. Oh, I should say, the lads call me Whistler now, which is not a nickname I wanted.
Ha. You work on a building site, then?
Fifteen years now. Brickwork mostly, outdoors all day, which is why the cold gets me. My brother-in-law keeps telling me to get a desk job, but I'd be bored stiff.
And do you smoke?
I know, I know. About ten cigarettes a day, I keep saying I'll cut down. Actually, I did cut down in January, then I had a bad week.
We'll come back to that, but first the immediate problem. Any previous chest trouble? Anything on your record you'd mention?
Asthma, since I was a boy. It was quiet for years but it's been waking up with this cold weather.
And what do you use for it?

The brown inhaler, twice a day, in the morning and at night. Though I missed a few days this week because I left it in my other jacket. I've got the blue one as well but that's actually my mate's, I borrowed it, so ignore that.
Right, so the brown one is yours, thank you. Do you have any allergies to medicines or anything else?
No, none at all. Not even hay fever, which is a miracle on a building site.
Doctor, his oxygen's 94 on air, and I've got the monitor reading a pulse of 104.
Thank you. So oxygen saturation is 94 percent, pulse 104, and his breathing rate is 22. A bit fast, but he's talking in full sentences, which is reassuring.
I always talk in full sentences. My wife says it's my only exercise.
Open your shirt for me, I'm going to listen to your chest now. Big breaths in and out through your mouth.
There's a clear wheeze through both lungs, more at the bases, and air is going in reasonably well.
Is that the asthma then? Or is it something worse, like my heart? I read something online and now I can't unread it.
This looks most likely like an asthma flare brought on by the cold, but with your age and smoking, I want to make sure we're not missing anything. That's why I'd like to get a chest X-ray done today.
I'll ring down to radiology and ask them to take him straight away.
Thank you. And Sam, please get a peak flow reading as well, so we can see how tight it is. We'll do that now.
Is that the thing you blow into? I'm rubbish at that, I'll blow the roof off.
That's the one, big deep breath in, seal your lips round it, then blow out as hard and fast as you can, like blowing out birthday candles.
Right. Like an eighty-year-old's cake, then. Ready?
While Sam sets up, take two puffs of your own inhaler, the brown one.
Oh, doctor, that one's the preventer. Isn't the blue one the one for emergencies? I've got confused. I'm sorry, my brain is all over the place today.
You're right to ask, and it's the blue one that's the reliever. Don't take any more of the borrowed one, though. We'll sort out the right reliever for you before you leave.
Good, because my mate will want it back, he gets it free from his doctor and he's very protective.
Ready when you are, let's try that blow.
Right, go ahead. Then I'll want you to rest for an hour or two while we wait for the picture, and I'll come and check on you again.
Thank you, doctor. And Sam. I'll try the smoking again, I promise. Probably.
Probably is a start. Sit back and breathe slowly.
